title_en: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation
author: Basil of Caesarea
addressee: His congregation at Caesarea in Cappadocia
occasion: Basil delivered these sermons to explain the Genesis creation account, counter pagan philosophical and heretical readings, and lead his hearers from visible creation to knowledge of the Creator. The source does not specify they were delivered during Lent or in a single season.
argument: Basil expounds Genesis 1:1–26 in nine homilies. He insists the world had a beginning and was made by God, not by chance or from eternal matter. He generally follows the literal sense but explicitly rejects only certain allegorical excesses; he allows spiritual applications and typological readings when appropriate, and insists on the plain meaning of the text against forced philosophical interpretations. He explains each day's work: light, firmament, gathered waters, vegetation, heavenly bodies, water creatures and birds, and land animals. Throughout, he draws moral lessons from nature and argues that the plural 'Let us make man' reveals the Father speaking to the Son.

outline.move: Homily 1: Basil introduces Moses as trustworthy author and expounds 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth,' arguing the world had a temporal beginning and was made by God's will.
Homily 2: He explains why the earth was 'invisible and unformed,' refutes the idea of eternal matter, and treats the creation of light and the first day.
Homily 3: He discusses the firmament, its nature and purpose, and rejects allegorical interpretations of the waters above the heavens.
Homily 4: He explains the gathering of the waters and the appearance of dry land, praising the sea's usefulness and order.
Homily 5: He treats the earth's bringing forth vegetation, showing God's provision and drawing moral lessons from plants and trees.
Homily 6: He explains the creation of the sun, moon, and stars, refutes astrology, and shows their purposes for signs, seasons, days, and years.
Homily 7: He treats the creation of water creatures, describing their variety and drawing moral lessons from their behaviors.

Homily 8: Basil covers both water creatures and birds together, explicitly noting he must go back to cover the birds he skipped in his previous discussion of water creatures, and uses them to teach providence, parental care, and moral lessons.
Homily 9: He discusses land animals, their natural wisdom and design, and begins the account of man's creation, arguing the plural 'Let us make man' indicates the Father and Son.

cast.name: Basil of Caesarea

cast.name: Paul

cast.who: The prophet, cited on the nature of heaven and human frailty.

cast.who: Cited for the saying 'Light is always for the righteous.'

cast.who: Patriarch, cited for his words about the days of his life.

cast.who: Heretic whose followers are mentioned as misinterpreting darkness.

cast.who: Heretic whose followers are mentioned as misinterpreting darkness.

cast.name: Manichaeans
cast.who: Heretical group accused of teaching that the earth has a soul.

cast.who: Egyptian king who first attempted to join the Red Sea to the Mediterranean.

cast.name: Darius the Mede
cast.who: King who later attempted the same canal project.

cast.name: Elisha

key_terms.sense: God's act of creating, emphasizing deliberate making rather than emanation or chance
The temporal beginning of the world, indicating it is not eternal
The firmament or expanse separating waters above from waters below
The heavenly lights, sun and moon, created on the fourth day
Living soul or living creature, used for animals as distinct from plants
According to kind, indicating fixed natural kinds in reproduction
The initial state of the earth, hidden by water and not yet furnished
The deep water covering the earth at creation, not a hostile power
Darkness as absence of light, not an independent evil principle
The Holy Spirit, active in creation and hovering over the waters
Image, used of man's creation in the image of God and of the Son as image of the Father
Likeness, the goal of human moral progress toward God
Astrology, the false art of predicting life from birth stars, which Basil refutes
Allegorical interpretation, which Basil rejects when it denies the literal sense of creation
The Only-begotten Son, the co-worker with the Father in creation

scripture: Basil quotes the Septuagint (LXX) and follows its book names and Psalm numbering. He cites Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Joel, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Ephesians, Colossians, Hebrews, and Revelation. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and LXX Psalm numbering, noting where it differs from the Hebrew (e.g., LXX Psalm 18 = Hebrew Psalm 19).
uncertain: The exact date of delivery; c. 378 is traditional but not certain.
Whether the homilies were delivered in a single Lenten season or over multiple years.
The precise identity of the 'Syrian man' whose interpretation Basil cites in Homily 2.
The exact geographical knowledge Basil relied on for his lists of rivers and seas.
Whether Basil had direct access to all the pagan philosophical works he critiques or knew them through doxographies.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He generally follows the literal sense but explicitly rejects only certain allegorical excesses; he allows spiritual applications and typological readings when appropriate
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πᾶσαν οὖν τροπικὴν καὶ δι' ὑπονοίας ἐξήγησιν ἔν γε τῷ παρόντι κατασιγάσαντες, τοῦ σκότους τὴν ἔννοιαν ἁπλῶς καὶ ἀπεριεργάστως, ἑπόμενοι τῷ βουλήματι τῆς Γραφῆς, ἐκδεξώμεθα (section 13); Οἱ μὲν γὰρ κατηναγκασμένον τὸ πιθανὸν τοῖς λόγοις ἐπάγουσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὲ γυμνὴ τεχνασμάτων ἡ ἀλήθεια πρόκειται (section 25); Ἐγὼ δὲ χόρτον ἀκούσας, χόρτον νοῶ, καὶ φυτὸν, καὶ ἰχθὺν, καὶ θηρίον, καὶ κτῆνος, πάντα ὡς εἴρηται οὕτως ἐκδέχομαι (section 69)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Basil explicitly rejects allegorical and tropological interpretations in favor of the plain literal sense throughout; he does not 'allow spiritual applications and typological readings when appropriate' but insists on the literal meaning of the text against forced philosophical and allegorical interpretations.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Homily 8: Basil covers both water creatures and birds together, explicitly noting he must go back to cover the birds he skipped in his previous discussion of water creatures
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Διέφυγεν ἡμᾶς τὸ πτηνὸν ἐν τῷ μέσῳ. Ἀνάγκη τοίνυν... ὑποστρέφουσιν... οὕτω καὶ ἡμῖν, ὡς ἔοικε, τὴν αὐτὴν πάλιν βαδιστέον (section 62); Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν, καὶ πετεινὰ πετόμενα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (section 62)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Homily 8: Basil explicitly notes he skipped the birds in Homily 7 and must go back to cover them; he discusses birds first (as the third element of creation he had omitted), then moves to land animals, not water creatures and birds together.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Elisha... Mentioned as someone who was not rejected as a poor host despite serving wild vegetables to his friends; Basil uses him to defend his own humble offering.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὐδὲ γὰρ Ἐλισσαῖον ὡς φαῦλον ἑστιάτορα παρῃτοῦντο οἱ τότε, καὶ ταῦτα λαχάνοις ἀγρίοις ἑστιῶντα τοὺς φίλους (section 69)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Elisha... Mentioned as someone whose friends did not reject him as a poor host even though he served them wild vegetables; Basil uses this to defend his own humble spiritual offering, not a literal meal.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the Egyptian Sea: the Mediterranean Sea
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸ Αἰγύπτιον καὶ τὸ Ἰνδικὸν, ἐν ᾧ ἡ ἐρυθρά ἐστι θάλασσα (section 29)
_unresolved_facts.fix: the Egyptian Sea: the Red Sea (not the Mediterranean); Basil explicitly identifies the Egyptian Sea with the Red Sea (ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα).
Remove 'the Bithynian land' from the names list; the source mentions 'τὴν Βιθυνῶν χώραν' in section 30 as part of a list of regions with lakes, not as a named entity requiring special identification.
Remove 'the Palestinian land' from the names list; the source mentions 'τὴν Παλαιστινῶν' in section 30 as part of a list of regions with lakes, not as a named entity requiring special identification.
